title: ANNUAL REPORT ON FORM 10-K FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDED JANUARY 31, 2022
summary: Walmart Inc.’s fiscal 2022 annual report covers the year ended January 31, 2022. References to Walmart Inc., Walmart, the Company, and related first-person terms refer to the Delaware corporation and, unless otherwise specified or required by context, its consolidated subsidiaries; this applies to the report, incorporated proxy-statement information, and exhibits.

title: PART I

nodes.title: Cautionary Statement Regarding Forward-Looking Statements
nodes.summary: Walmart’s 10-K explains that its SEC filings, public announcements, and presentations may contain forward-looking statements protected by securities-law safe harbors. These are estimates, expectations, plans, goals, or assumptions—not historical facts—and may concern financial and operating performance, growth, investments, workforce, currency, shareholder returns, liquidity, taxes, litigation, accounting standards, ESG commitments, and strategy. Identified by predictive language, they rely on current knowledge and assumptions; actual outcomes may differ due to disclosed or unknown risks and changing circumstances. Walmart cautions against undue reliance, says statements speak only as of their dates, and generally disclaims any duty to update them.

nodes.title: ITEM 1. BUSINESS
The Development of Our Company
nodes.summary: Walmart describes its global retail and eCommerce business, customer-focused omnichannel strategy, everyday-low-price and cost-control commitments, three reporting segments, fiscal-year basis, fiscal 2022 revenue, headquarters and stock listing. It recounts company milestones from its founders’ variety stores through Sam’s Club, supercenters, Neighborhood Markets, international expansion and eCommerce, including pickup and delivery growth and Flipkart. Walmart highlights its stores, technology, marketplaces, supply chain and workforce as an integrated customer flywheel, supported by Walmart+, advertising, fulfillment, health and financial services.

nodes.title: Information About Our Segments
nodes.summary: The company operates retail, wholesale, and eCommerce businesses across the U.S., Africa, Canada, Central America, Chile, China, India, and Mexico. It sold its Argentina operations in fiscal 2021 and its U.K. and Japan operations in the first quarter of fiscal 2022; details are in Note 12. Its three reportable segments are Walmart U.S., Walmart International, and Sam’s Club. Each contributes differently but has generally maintained a consistent share of net sales and operating income, with minor currency-related changes for Walmart International. Further segment and geographic details appear in Note 13.

nodes.title: Walmart U.S. Segment
nodes.summary: Walmart U.S., operating across all 50 states, Washington, D.C., and Puerto Rico under Walmart and Neighborhood Market brands and online, is the company’s largest segment, accounting for 69% of fiscal 2022 sales ($393.2 billion) and historically leading in gross profit rate, sales, and operating income. It integrates stores and eCommerce through pickup, delivery, ship-from-store, pharmacy fulfillment, Walmart+, and digital platforms; store formats and approximate sizes are detailed. Merchandise spans grocery, general merchandise, and health and wellness, including national, private, and licensed brands; prior-period category figures may be revised for comparability. Other offerings include Walmart Connect advertising, marketplace fulfillment, Walmart Health, GoLocal delivery, Luminate data products, fuel, and financial services, which are not yet significant revenue sources. Operations, seasonal sales patterns, extensive competition, competitive factors and strategies (EDLP, EDLC, omnichannel convenience, and service expansion), and a 157-facility distribution network, private fleet, carriers, fulfillment centers, and store-based shipping are described.

nodes.title: Walmart International Segment
nodes.summary: Walmart International, its second-largest segment, operated in 23 countries as of January 2022 through wholly and majority-owned subsidiaries; the text describes its country footprint and recent divestitures in Argentina, the U.K. and Japan. It covers retail, wholesale and eCommerce formats, sales and lower gross margins, and a strategy focused on locally relevant, profitable growth. It outlines omnichannel services, store sizes and pickup/delivery capacity; merchandise, private brands, suppliers and ancillary financial, payment and advertising services; operating hours, technology and seasonality; competitive pressures and emphasis on price leadership and food operations; and distribution networks, fulfillment centers and shipping methods.

nodes.title: Sam's Club Segment
nodes.summary: Sam’s Club’s U.S. and Puerto Rico operations, sales, membership fees and benefits, Sam’s Cash rewards, omnichannel services, facilities, merchandise categories, private label, hours, technology, seasonality, competition, and distribution are described. The text also covers protections and licensing of intellectual property; global supplier relationships, standards, and supply-chain effects on product availability; compliance with U.S. and international regulation; and Walmart’s ESG approach, focused on shared value and four priorities: opportunity, sustainability, community, and ethics and integrity.

nodes.title: Sam’s Club Operations and Business Risks
nodes.summary: Sam’s Club experiences seasonal sales peaks in the quarter ending January 31 and competes across warehouse, retail, wholesale, fuel, and online channels through value, assortment, bulk sizing, and eCommerce. Its distribution network uses dedicated and Walmart facilities, fulfillment centers, suppliers, private trucks, and carriers. The company protects and licenses intellectual property; relies on global suppliers and logistics to sustain assortment, availability, and low prices, with supplier conduct standards; and operates under U.S. and foreign laws and regulations.

nodes.title: Environmental, Social and Governance ("ESG") Priorities
nodes.summary: Walmart’s ESG strategy seeks shared value and long-term competitive advantage by serving stakeholders and addressing societal needs, building trust, revenue, capabilities, and managing costs and risks. It prioritizes issues relevant to its business and where it can make a positive impact across four themes: opportunity (inclusive economic opportunity, diversity, equity, and inclusion); sustainability (responsible sourcing, labor protections, women’s empowerment, safer products, emissions reduction, nature protection, and waste reduction, including zero operational emissions by 2040 and one billion metric tons reduced or avoided in its value chain by 2030); community (affordable, healthier products, disaster support, volunteering, grants, and cohesion); and ethics and integrity (fostering trust). Walmart periodically updates ESG disclosures on its website, which are not incorporated into the 10-K.

nodes.title: Human Capital Management
nodes.summary: Walmart describes its 2.3 million-person global workforce and its focus on attracting, developing, rewarding, and retaining associates through career paths, training, competitive pay, benefits, and advancement; U.S. turnover rose after the pandemic. Its priorities are inclusion, including diversity representation, fair pay, and associate feedback; physical, emotional, and financial well-being, including U.S. benefits, health and safety measures, vaccine access, and COVID leave; growth through career development, training, and education programs; and digital transformation through tools, eCommerce roles, and technology-based solutions.

nodes.title: Information About Our Executive Officers
nodes.summary: The text lists Walmart’s executive officers as of the 10-K filing, noting they are appointed by and serve at the Board’s pleasure and that listed experience generally reflects their principal occupations over the prior five years. For Daniel Bartlett, Brett Biggs, Rachel Brand, David Chojnowski, John Furner, Suresh Kumar, Judith McKenna, Kathryn McLay, Doug McMillon, and Donna Morris, it gives age, year in their current position, role, effective date, and relevant prior roles and employers.

nodes.title: Our Website and Availability of SEC Reports and Other Information
nodes.summary: Walmart’s website provides free access, as soon as reasonably practicable after SEC submission, to its SEC reports and other filings; the SEC’s website also hosts issuer filings. Walmart’s filings, senior financial officers’ Reporting Protocols, and Code of Conduct are online and available in print to shareholders upon request through Investor Relations. Descriptions of substantive amendments or waivers to those protocols or the Code for the CEO, CFO, or principal accounting officer are posted under Corporate Governance for 12 months.

Describes Walmart’s history, global retail and eCommerce strategy, business segments, operations, offerings, competition, seasonal patterns, and distribution networks, including Walmart U.S., Walmart International, and Sam’s Club. Covers intellectual property, supplier relationships, regulatory compliance, ESG priorities and initiatives, workforce size and human-capital programs, executive officers and their backgrounds, and online availability of SEC filings, governance documents, and related disclosures.

nodes.title: ITEM 1A. RISK FACTORS

Strategic Risks Failure to successfully execute our omni-channel strategy and the cost of our investments in eCommerce and technology may materially adversely affect our market position, net sales and financial performance.
nodes.summary: The company warns that listed and other U.S. and global risks could materially harm its business, results, financial position, and liquidity, and that the risks are not exhaustive. Retail is rapidly shifting to digital shopping. Its costly omnichannel strategy—including investments in eCommerce, technology, talent, automation, acquisitions, partnerships, and store remodels—may fail to grow sales, market position, or customer relationships and offset slower store openings. Failure to execute interconnected initiatives could cause financial harm and asset impairments; increased online grocery and eCommerce sales may divert store traffic and cross-selling. Investment costs and operating losses may hurt short-term results, while unrealized benefits may hurt long-term performance.

nodes.title: If we do not timely identify or effectively respond to consumer trends or preferences, it could negatively affect our relationship with our customers, demand for the products and services we sell, our market share and the growth of our business.
nodes.summary: The text identifies risks from failing to anticipate or respond to changing consumer tastes, shopping habits, and ESG preferences, including effects on customer relationships, demand, market share, and growth. It describes intense, evolving competition across retail and related services, competitive factors, innovation and execution risks, and how industry consolidation or alliances can strengthen rivals. It also explains how domestic and global economic conditions may weaken demand, margins, sales, inventory turnover, and operations, increase costs, disrupt suppliers, and trigger asset impairments. Finally, strategic alliances and business relationships may underperform expectations or weaken business and competitive position.

nodes.title: Competition and Economic Risks
key_items: We face strong competition from other retailers, wholesale club operators, omni-channel retailers, and other businesses which could materially adversely affect our financial performance.
General or macro-economic factors, both domestically and internationally, may materially adversely affect our financial performance.
nodes.summary: The page explains how intense, evolving competition across physical, digital, and omni-channel retail and related services—including new entrants, innovation, and industry consolidation—could weaken the company’s position and financial performance if it fails to respond effectively. It also describes how domestic and international economic conditions, including inflation, interest rates, employment, consumer spending and credit, energy and operating costs, taxes, regulation, trade barriers, currency changes, and recession, may reduce demand and margins, slow inventory turnover, increase markdowns and expenses, impair assets, and disrupt suppliers.

nodes.title: The performance of strategic alliances and other business relationships to support the expansion of our business could materially adversely affect our financial performance.
nodes.summary: Strategic alliances and other business relationships in current or new markets may fail to deliver anticipated sales, harm the business or competitive position compared with operating without them, and related investments—including in recently divested markets—could materially adversely affect financial performance.

nodes.title: Operational Risks The impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on our business, financial position and results of operations continues to be unpredictable, and we may be unable to sustain our revenue growth rate in the future.
nodes.summary: COVID-19’s unpredictable course, including resurgences and variants, may disrupt operations, demand, inventory, supply chains, costs, restrictions, forecasting, litigation exposure, and financial results. Changing customer behavior may make demand and inventory harder to predict, causing stockouts and delivery delays. Outcomes also depend on pandemic severity and duration, macroeconomic conditions, response investments, vaccination and treatment effectiveness, recovery pace, and lasting behavioral changes. Pandemic-driven revenue and eCommerce growth may not persist; as conditions subside, failure to capture opportunities could reduce revenue and results. Ongoing economic effects may intensify risks involving customers, competition, reputation, strategy, cybersecurity, payments, technology, supply chains, labor, litigation, and regulation.

nodes.title: Natural disasters, climate change, geopolitical events, global health epidemics or pandemics and catastrophic events could materially adversely affect our financial performance.
nodes.summary: Natural disasters, severe weather and climate change, geopolitical conflict, pandemics, violence, and other catastrophes may damage facilities or inventory, interrupt stores, digital services, staffing, transport, utilities, communications and supply chains, alter consumer behavior and costs, and materially harm financial performance. Climate risks include physical impacts on facilities, commodities and communities, and transition impacts from price, market, stakeholder and regulatory changes. Supplier-related risks include instability, noncompliance, labor and raw-material shortages, quality and transport disruptions, currency, inflation, tariffs and sanctions. Unsafe products can cause customer losses, liability and reputational damage. Third-party marketplace sales also pose legal, compliance, counterfeit and other reputational and financial risks that may hinder eCommerce growth.

nodes.title: Operational, Supplier, Product, and Marketplace Risks
key_items: Risks associated with our suppliers could materially adversely affect our financial performance.

If the products we sell are not safe or otherwise fail to meet our customers' expectations, we could lose customers, incur liability for any injuries suffered by customers using or consuming a product we sell or otherwise experience a material impact to our brand, reputation and financial performance. We are also subject to reputational and other risks related to third-party sales on our digital platforms.
nodes.summary: The page describes risks from infrastructure and climate-related disruptions, including damage, inventory loss, higher costs, and interrupted operations. Supplier instability, labor and sourcing issues, transport disruption, tariffs, sanctions, and other trade factors could limit product access and harm financial performance. Unsafe or disappointing products may drive customers away, create liability, and damage reputation. Third-party marketplace sales also pose legal, reputational, financial, and competitive risks, potentially hindering eCommerce growth.

nodes.title: Information Systems and Digital Commerce Risks
key_items: We rely extensively on information systems to process transactions, summarize results and manage our business. Disruptions in our systems could harm our ability to conduct our operations.

If the technology-based systems that give our customers the ability to shop with us online do not function effectively, our operating results, as well as our ability to grow our omni-channel business globally, could be materially adversely affected.
nodes.summary: The company depends on business-critical information systems and online platforms for transactions, operations, and global omnichannel growth. Outages, disasters, errors, cyberattacks, incomplete recovery plans, and technology upgrades may disrupt operations, compromise or corrupt data, and require costly repairs. Digital platforms must keep pace with customer expectations and competition through secure, convenient shopping, broad selection, and rapid, low-cost fulfillment. Failures or attacks could disrupt services and supply chains, expose customer information, reduce sales, damage reputation and competitiveness, create liability, and harm business results and strategy.

nodes.title: Any failure to maintain the privacy or security of the information relating to our company, customers, members, associates and vendors, whether as a result of cyberattacks on our information systems or otherwise, could damage our reputation, result in litigation or other legal actions against us, cause us to incur substantial additional costs, and materially adversely affect our business and operating results.
nodes.summary: The text describes the company’s exposure to cyber and privacy risks involving customer, member, associate, vendor, health, payment and other confidential data held by the company and third parties. Evolving attacks, remote work, human error, and technology vulnerabilities may cause breaches or disruptions that are difficult to detect or prevent. Consequences include operational and sales losses, reputational and competitive harm, litigation, remediation costs, and regulatory penalties, including under HIPAA, privacy, payment-card, consumer-finance, anti-money-laundering and sanctions rules. Payment services create additional compliance and liability risks; insurance and existing security, compliance and risk-management measures may not prevent or cover losses.

nodes.title: Changes in the results of our health and wellness business could adversely affect our overall results of operations, cash flows and liquidity.
nodes.summary: Walmart’s retail pharmacies and Walmart Health services face risks that could harm overall results, cash flows and liquidity. Pharmacy risks include changes in reimbursement rates, payer mix and formularies; network access; drug costs, availability and mix; administrative burdens; insurance and government programs; competition, consolidation and economic conditions; customer payment ability; performance thresholds; financial-assistance rules; and regulatory or legislative changes. Pharmaceutical supply disruptions could damage reputation and drive customers to competitors. These factors may reduce sales volumes, increase costs, lower pharmacy sales and margins, and diminish cross-store or cross-club sales.

nodes.title: Our failure to attract and retain qualified associates, increases in wage and benefit costs, changes in laws and other labor issues could materially adversely affect our financial performance.
nodes.summary: The text explains that labor shortages, retention challenges, wage and benefit increases, labor or healthcare law changes, and unsuccessful organizational or leadership transitions could reduce service quality and materially harm financial performance. It also warns that missing market expectations for sales, income, spending, comparable-store and e-commerce growth, margins, or earnings—or changes to dividends, buybacks, tax rates, analyst estimates, or performance versus retailers—could lower the stock price and increase volatility.

nodes.title: Fluctuations in foreign exchange rates may materially adversely affect our financial performance and our reported results of operations.
nodes.summary: Unfavorable foreign exchange movements can distort translated financial results, harm Walmart International and consolidated performance, and raise costs on products purchased in other currencies when prices cannot be adjusted, reducing gross profit. International operations—about 18% of fiscal 2022 net sales across numerous countries—face political, economic, legal, regulatory, tax, labor, trade, currency, competition, product-safety, environmental, data-protection, inflation, and other risks, plus management, tax, and intellectual-property challenges across jurisdictions. Associates, contractors, or agents may violate anti-corruption laws despite company policies and compliance programs, risking financial, business, and reputational harm.

nodes.title: Changes in tax and trade laws and regulations could materially adversely affect our financial performance.
nodes.summary: Changes in trade policies, tariffs, and regulations could raise costs and selling prices for imported merchandise, harming Walmart’s U.S. operations; its U.S. and Sam’s Club segments generated about 82% of fiscal 2022 sales. Domestic and foreign tax-law, rate, regulatory, and accounting changes—and uncertainty in tax estimates, deferred tax valuations, and jurisdictional earnings—could increase compliance costs and materially affect the effective tax rate, financial position, results, or cash flows. Tax-authority audits may also produce outcomes differing materially from recorded estimates.

nodes.title: Changes in and/or failure to comply with other laws, regulations, and interpretations of such laws and regulations specific to the businesses and jurisdictions in which we operate could materially adversely affect our reputation, market position, or our business and financial performance.
nodes.summary: The text warns that evolving laws, regulations, interpretations, enforcement, and scrutiny across the U.S. and other operating jurisdictions may increase costs, require operational changes, damage reputation, or harm business and financial performance. It covers extensive requirements involving pharmacy and controlled substances, health care and government reimbursement, product safety, privacy and cybersecurity, environmental and workplace matters, consumer and financial services, fraud, sanctions, competition, labor, and ESG disclosures. Privacy laws impose broad duties, consumer rights, and potentially substantial penalties. Audits or noncompliance may lead to fines, criminal or civil liability, lost licenses or certifications, government-program exclusion or suspended payments, and terminated supplier or payer contracts; even unsuccessful challenges can cause adverse publicity and costly defenses.

nodes.title: We are subject to risks related to litigation and other legal proceedings that may materially adversely affect our results of operations, financial position and liquidity.
nodes.summary: The company faces extensive litigation, regulatory investigations and possible indemnification obligations that could harm results, finances and liquidity; cases may be costly, lengthy and seek large or punitive damages. Matters include wage-and-hour and consumer class actions; opioid-related government inquiries and nationwide litigation, including MDL proceedings, a dismissed and unsuccessfully appealed company declaratory action, a DOJ CSA enforcement suit stayed pending Supreme Court cases, a securities class action, and shareholder derivative suits. The company cannot predict future opioid claims or estimate potential losses and refers readers to its legal-proceedings disclosures and financial-statement notes. Bylaws make Delaware Chancery the exclusive forum for specified shareholder claims, potentially increasing costs, discouraging claims or limiting forum choice; unenforceability could add costs. The provision does not waive or restrict federal securities-law jurisdiction.

nodes.title: Our reputation may be adversely affected if we are not able to achieve our ESG goals.
nodes.summary: The company pursues ESG goals and shared value amid stakeholder expectations, periodically announcing aspirations and publishing its priorities, strategies, and progress online. Goals involve risks and factors beyond its control; it may fail or be perceived to fail, and stakeholders may consider its efforts inadequate. ESG reporting discusses some challenges but is not part of or incorporated into the 10-K. Actual or perceived shortfalls could harm reputation, employee morale, and customer or shareholder support.

The section outlines strategic, operational, financial, legal, and reputational risks that could harm Walmart’s business, results, financial position, or liquidity. These include failure to execute costly omnichannel and technology investments; changing customer preferences, competition, economic conditions, alliances, and pandemic effects; disasters, climate, geopolitical and supply-chain disruptions; product and marketplace risks; information-system, cybersecurity, and privacy failures; health-business performance; labor challenges; currency, international, tax, trade, regulatory, and litigation exposure; missed financial expectations; and failure to meet ESG goals. Risks may increase costs, reduce demand, sales, margins, or market share, disrupt operations, and cause liabilities or reputational damage.

Mine safety disclosures are not applicable.

title: ITEM 7. MANAGEMENT'S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS

nodes.title: ITEM 7. MANAGEMENT'S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS (intro)
nodes.summary: The MD&A explains its purpose, fiscal years covered, segment measures, comparable-sales methodology and currency calculations. It notes international portfolio sales (Argentina, Asda and Seiyu) and their losses, intense competition, factors affecting results, and ongoing COVID-19 and economic uncertainty. Walmart’s financial framework emphasizes efficient growth, operating discipline and strategic capital allocation, with growth focused on existing-store sales, eCommerce and omnichannel initiatives. U.S. comparable sales rose 7.7% in fiscal 2022 and 8.7% in 2021; Walmart U.S. rose 6.4% and 8.7%, while Sam’s Club rose 15.0% and 8.7%. Growth drivers included tickets, transactions, stimulus and inflation; tobacco removal and fuel affected Sam’s Club, while eCommerce contributed to both businesses’ comparable sales.

nodes.title: Company Performance and Comparable Sales
nodes.summary: The page notes economic, operating, and pandemic-related uncertainties and directs readers to risk factors and segment results. Walmart’s financial framework emphasizes strong, efficient growth, operating discipline, and strategic capital allocation to improve returns. Growth priorities include comparable sales, eCommerce, and complementary omnichannel initiatives, with slower new-store expansion and selective long-term investment. It defines calendar versus retail-calendar comparable sales and reports fiscal 2022/2021 results: U.S. sales rose 7.7%/8.7%, Walmart U.S. 6.4%/8.7%, and Sam’s Club 15.0%/8.7%. Drivers included ticket, transaction, stimulus, inflation, pandemic behavior, fuel, tobacco removals, and eCommerce contributions.

nodes.title: Operating Discipline and Capital Allocation
nodes.summary: The page describes cost discipline through expense management, productivity, inventory control, technology and process improvements, measured by sales growth relative to operating expense growth. Fiscal 2022 operating expenses fell to 20.8% of sales, down 19 basis points, benefiting from comparable sales growth and $2.5 billion less in incremental COVID-19 costs, partly offset by wage investments; fiscal 2021 was flat, with sales growth offset by $4.0 billion in pandemic costs. Capital allocation prioritizes supply chain, omni-channel initiatives, technology and remodels over new locations; a table compares 2021 and 2022 spending by category and U.S. and International totals.

nodes.title: Returns
key_items: Return on Assets and Return on Investment
nodes.summary: Walmart expects returns on capital to improve and describes share repurchases and dividends as additional shareholder returns. It reports ROA of 5.6% in fiscal 2022 and 2021, and non-GAAP ROI of 14.9% and 14.0%, respectively, explaining their definitions, adjustments, limitations, calculation methods, and reconciliations. It also defines non-GAAP free cash flow, reports operating cash flow and free cash flow for fiscal 2020–2022, explains year-over-year changes, cautions that the measure excludes debt service, contractual obligations, and acquisitions, and reconciles it to GAAP operating cash flow alongside investing and financing cash flows.

nodes.title: Results of Operations
nodes.summary: Reports Walmart’s consolidated and segment results for fiscal 2022, 2021 and 2020, including revenues, sales, comparable sales, margins, operating income, debt extinguishment, other gains and losses, net income, EPS, taxes, store counts and square footage. Explains consolidated performance drivers: consumer demand, inflation, currency, COVID-19 effects, U.K. and Japan divestitures, pricing, merchandise mix, supply-chain costs, wages and equity investment valuations. Details Walmart U.S., International and Sam’s Club sales, gross profit, expenses and operating income, including e-commerce, membership, fuel and tobacco effects, pandemic costs, and relevant segment-specific factors. Notes unit-count exclusions and why Sam’s Club results excluding fuel are presented.

nodes.title: Liquidity and Capital Resources Liquidity
Liquidity and Capital Resources Liquidity (intro)
nodes.summary: The company says stable operations, operating cash flow, long- and short-term borrowing have funded operations and growth investments, with remaining cash generally supporting dividends and share repurchases. It expects liquidity to cover operations, global investments, dividends and repurchases for at least 12 months and the foreseeable future. Operating cash flow was $24.2 billion in fiscal 2022, $36.1 billion in 2021 and $25.3 billion in 2020. The 2022 decline reflected higher inventory costs and purchases to support strong sales, comparison with accelerated 2021 inventory sell-through, and wage timing; 2021’s increase reflected the health crisis, inventory sell-through and purchase timing, COVID-related costs, and benefit payments.

nodes.title: Cash Equivalents and Working Capital Deficit
nodes.summary: Cash and cash equivalents were $14.8 billion in 2022 versus $17.7 billion in 2021; working capital deficits were $6.3 billion and $2.6 billion, reflecting efficient cash use, capital-market access, dividends, and share repurchases. Intercompany financing and occasional foreign-earnings repatriation help place cash where needed. U.S. tax reform generally removes federal tax on repatriation, though other taxes may apply; restrictions are not expected to materially affect the company, and restricted cash was $4.3 billion in 2022 versus $2.8 billion in 2021, including $2.2 billion subject to Flipkart minority-shareholder approval and expected to be used by Flipkart. Investing cash outflows were $6.0 billion, $10.1 billion, and $9.1 billion in fiscal 2022, 2021, and 2020, mainly for capital expenditures. The 2022 decrease reflected Asda and Seiyu divestiture proceeds, partly offset by higher capital spending; the 2021 increase reflected lapping Walmart Canada banking-sale proceeds and other investing changes, partly offset by lower capital spending.

nodes.title: Capital expenditures
nodes.summary: The text projects fiscal 2023 capital expenditures of about $18 billion, focused on supply chain, automation, customer initiatives and technology. It reports financing cash flows for 2020–2022 and explains year-over-year changes, including debt repayments, premiums, borrowings, share repurchases and Flipkart equity funding that reduced Walmart’s stake from 83% to 75%. It details short-term borrowing levels, rates, credit lines and letters of credit; fiscal 2022 long-term debt movements, extinguishment costs and estimated interest payments; and dividend payments for 2020–2022 plus the approved fiscal 2023 dividend increase to $2.24 per share, paid quarterly.

nodes.title: Short-Term Borrowings and Long-Term Debt
nodes.summary: The page describes financing cash-flow changes, including fiscal 2021 increases in cash used and fiscal 2022 Flipkart equity funding that reduced Walmart’s ownership from 83% to 75%. It reports short-term borrowing activity and rates for 2020–2022, year-end balances and rates, available U.S. and international credit facilities, and letters of credit. It also details fiscal 2022 long-term debt movements, the $6.6 billion decrease, debt issuance and early extinguishment, related premiums and losses, and estimated contractual interest payments.

nodes.title: Dividends
nodes.summary: The text reports annual dividends of $6.0–$6.2 billion for fiscal 2020–2022 and a fiscal 2023 dividend increase to $2.24 per share, paid quarterly at $0.56 with specified record and payment dates. It describes the $20 billion share repurchase program, remaining authorization, decision factors, expected funding, fiscal 2023 spending plans, and repurchase totals and average prices for 2020–2022. It outlines operating and contractual cash requirements, including $27.9 billion in purchase obligations ($9.3 billion due within a year), and states that cash, borrowing capacity, capital markets, and strong debt ratings should meet obligations and support refinancing.

nodes.title: Share Repurchases and Material Cash Requirements
nodes.summary: The page lists 2022 dividend record and payable dates, then describes the Company’s share repurchase programs, remaining $10.6 billion authorization, factors guiding repurchases, expected funding, planned fiscal 2023 spending of at least $10 billion, and fiscal 2020–2022 share repurchase totals and average prices. It also outlines operating cash needs and contractual obligations, including $27.9 billion in purchase obligations ($9.3 billion due within one year), their scope and exclusions, and variability in payment timing and amounts.

The section reviews liquidity sources, operating cash flow trends and their drivers, cash balances, working capital deficits, restricted cash, and investing outflows. It describes capital spending plans; financing cash flows, short- and long-term debt, borrowing facilities, interest costs and payments; dividend history and increases; and share-repurchase authorization, activity, funding and plans. It also outlines purchase obligations and other cash requirements, and explains why cash, borrowing capacity, capital-market access and debt ratings are expected to fund operations, investments, distributions and obligations.

nodes.title: Capital Resources
nodes.summary: The company expects operating cash flows, cash on hand, short-term borrowing and capital-market access to cover anticipated obligations, including seasonal inventory, capital spending, acquisitions, dividends and share repurchases. Its January 31, 2022 ratings were S&P A-1+/AA, Moody’s P-1/Aa2 and Fitch F1+/AA for commercial paper/long-term debt, supporting refinancing at favorable rates. Ratings can change based on business, economic, retail, financial or strategic factors; downgrades could raise borrowing costs, limit market access or reduce commercial-paper flexibility, forcing more expensive financing. Ratings are not investment recommendations and may be revised or withdrawn; each applies only to its specified security and should be assessed independently.

nodes.title: Other Matters
nodes.summary: The report describes contingencies in Note 10, including prescription opioid litigation and related risks, and the company’s indemnification obligation for Asda Equal Value Claims. It references legal proceedings covering federal and state opioid litigation, DOJ opioid civil litigation, opioid-related securities class actions and derivative litigation, Asda claims, money transfer agent services, foreign direct investment, and a California environmental matter. These matters may or may not result in material liabilities when resolved.

nodes.title: Summary of Critical Accounting Estimates
Inventories
nodes.summary: U.S. GAAP financial statements require management estimates and judgments based on past events and expected outcomes; actual results may differ. Management regularly reviews accounting policies and disclosures. Inventory is valued at the lower of cost or market, primarily using the retail method: Walmart U.S. uses LIFO, while Sam’s Club uses weighted-average cost LIFO. Estimated inflation provisions rely on inventory levels, markups, and internal price indices, then are adjusted to year-end actuals. A 1% increase in retail price indices would not reduce inventory’s carrying value, and LIFO inventory approximated FIFO value at January 31, 2022 and 2021.

nodes.title: Asset Impairment, Acquisition Accounting, and Contingencies
key_items: Business Combinations, Goodwill, and Acquired Intangible Assets
nodes.summary: The page explains impairment reviews for long-lived assets, including cash-flow-based assessments, sensitivity, and material charges from fiscal 2021 divestitures and fiscal 2022 closings. It describes acquisition-method accounting, fair-value estimates, goodwill assignment, and annual or event-driven impairment testing, noting fiscal 2020 charges for trade names and software. It also outlines when legal losses are accrued or disclosed, quarterly reviews, and the potential material impact of unresolved proceedings.

nodes.title: Income Taxes
nodes.summary: Income taxes materially affect earnings, and provisions require judgment and estimates across U.S. and foreign jurisdictions. Effective rates fluctuate with tax contingencies, valuation allowances, law changes, audit outcomes, discrete items, and geographic earnings mix; audits may alter provisions. Uncertain tax benefits are recognized only when more likely than not to withstand challenge, using a minimum recognition threshold, and reassessed as facts change. Deferred tax assets arise from temporary differences and loss or credit carryforwards; valuation allowances reflect realization prospects based on earnings, forecasts, carryforward periods, reversals, and tax-planning strategies. Estimates are updated under applicable guidance as new regulations or standards are issued.

The section reviews critical accounting estimates and the judgments underlying U.S. GAAP statements, noting actual results may differ. It covers inventory valuation methods, inflation estimates, and LIFO/FIFO comparisons; impairment testing for long-lived assets and goodwill, acquisition fair-value estimates, and related charges; and legal contingency accruals and disclosures. It also explains income tax provision estimates, rate fluctuations, uncertain tax benefits, audits, deferred tax assets and valuation allowances, and updates for changing facts, laws, and standards.

summary: Explains Walmart’s MD&A scope, comparable-sales methods and results, strategy for efficient growth, operating discipline, capital allocation and shareholder returns. Reviews operating expenses, investments, returns on capital, free cash flow and reconciliations; fiscal 2020–2022 consolidated and segment performance and its drivers; liquidity, cash flows, debt, ratings, financing needs, dividends and repurchases; legal contingencies and proceedings; and critical accounting estimates for inventory, impairments, legal matters and income taxes.

title: ITEM 7A. QUANTITATIVE AND QUALITATIVE DISCLOSURES ABOUT MARKET RISK
summary: The disclosure describes exposure to interest-rate, foreign-currency, and equity-investment market risks, noting that sensitivity analyses use hypothetical scenarios and isolate each assumption. Interest-rate risk is managed through fixed/variable debt mix and swaps; swap fair value fell $0.2 billion in fiscal 2022. A maturity table details debt and swap cash flows and rates. Variable-rate borrowings were 22% of debt; a 100-basis-point rate change would alter annual interest costs by about $0.1 billion. Currency movements caused a $0.6 billion translation loss; currency swaps had liabilities of $1.0 billion versus $0.1 billion a year earlier. Hypothetical 10% dollar weakening or swap-rate changes would affect swap value by $1.0 billion or $40 million; immaterial forwards hedge some commitments. Equity investments lost $2.4 billion in value, were worth $11.9 billion, and a hypothetical 10% stock-price change would shift value by about $1.2 billion.

title: ITEM 8. FINANCIAL STATEMENTS AND SUPPLEMENTARY DATA
summary: Item 8 presents Walmart Inc.’s consolidated financial statements and supplementary data for the fiscal year ended January 31, 2022. The contents list the independent auditor’s reports on the financial statements and internal control, consolidated income and comprehensive income statements, balance sheets, shareholders’ equity and cash flows statements, and notes, with page references.

title: Report of Independent Registered Public Accounting Firm

nodes.title: Walmart Independent Auditor’s Report
nodes.summary: The auditor gives an unqualified opinion that Walmart’s 2022 and 2021 consolidated balance sheets and related financial statements for the three years ended January 31, 2022 fairly present the company’s finances under U.S. GAAP, and reports an unqualified opinion on 2022 internal controls. The report explains management’s responsibility, the auditor’s PCAOB registration and independence, and the audit’s risk-based procedures, evidence testing, and evaluation of accounting principles, estimates, and presentation, which provide a reasonable basis for the opinion.

nodes.title: Critical Audit Matter
nodes.summary: EY identifies legal contingencies as a critical audit matter because management’s assessments of loss probability and estimability involved complex judgment; this designation does not change its overall financial-statement opinion. Audit work included testing related controls, reviewing board minutes and counsel communications and opinions, discussing case status with internal legal counsel, and assessing disclosures. EY, Walmart’s auditor since 1969, also opines that internal control over financial reporting was effective in all material respects as of January 31, 2022, under COSO criteria. The report describes management and auditor responsibilities, audit procedures, the purpose and components of such controls, and their inherent limitations, including risks of undetected misstatement and future deterioration. EY’s report is dated March 18, 2022, in Rogers, Arkansas.

nodes.title: Walmart Internal Control Audit Opinion
key_items: Opinion on Internal Control over Financial Reporting
nodes.summary: The independent auditor concluded Walmart maintained effective internal control over financial reporting as of January 31, 2022, under COSO criteria, and noted an unqualified opinion on its audited financial statements. Management is responsible for the controls and its effectiveness assessment; the auditor, independent and PCAOB-registered, conducted a PCAOB-compliant audit to obtain reasonable assurance. Procedures included understanding controls, assessing material-weakness risk, testing design and operating effectiveness, and other necessary work.

nodes.title: Definition and Limitations of Internal Control over Financial Reporting
Definition and Limitations of Internal Control over Financial Reporting (intro)
nodes.summary: Defines internal control over financial reporting as providing reasonable assurance of reliable GAAP financial statements through accurate records, authorized transactions and expenditures, and prevention or timely detection of material unauthorized asset activity. Notes that controls may not prevent or detect misstatements and that future effectiveness can be undermined by changing conditions or reduced compliance. The statement is signed by Ernst & Young LLP in Rogers, Arkansas, on March 18, 2022.

nodes.title: Consolidated Statements of Income
nodes.summary: Walmart Inc.’s consolidated income statements for fiscal years ended January 31, 2022, 2021, and 2020, in millions except per-share data, report revenues from net sales and membership and other income; costs and expenses; operating income; interest, debt-extinguishment losses, and other gains or losses; pretax income, income taxes, consolidated net income and amounts attributable to noncontrolling interests and Walmart; basic and diluted earnings per share, weighted-average common shares, and dividends declared per share. The statements refer readers to accompanying notes.

nodes.title: Consolidated Statements of Comprehensive Income
nodes.summary: Walmart Inc.’s consolidated statements of comprehensive income report fiscal years ended January 31, 2020, 2021, and 2022, in millions. They present consolidated net income and amounts attributable to noncontrolling interests and Walmart; after-tax other comprehensive income or loss from currency translation and other items, net investment hedges, cash flow hedges, and minimum pension liability; related noncontrolling-interest and Walmart attributions; and comprehensive income and its attributions. The statements refer readers to accompanying notes.

nodes.title: Consolidated Balance Sheets
nodes.summary: Walmart Inc.’s consolidated balance sheets compare January 31, 2022 and 2021, in millions. They list current and noncurrent assets, including cash, receivables, inventory, property, lease assets, and goodwill; current and long-term liabilities, including borrowings, payables, debt, leases, and taxes; commitments and contingencies; and equity components, including common stock, retained earnings, accumulated comprehensive loss, and noncontrolling interest. Total assets and total liabilities and equity are reported for both years, with accompanying notes referenced.

nodes.title: Consolidated Statements of Shareholders' Equity
nodes.summary: Walmart Inc.’s consolidated shareholders’ equity statement reports balances at February 1, 2019, and January 31, 2020, 2021, and 2022. It presents common shares and par value, capital in excess of par, retained earnings, accumulated other comprehensive income or loss, Walmart shareholders’ equity, noncontrolling interest, and total equity. Changes include accounting-standard adoption, consolidated net income and other comprehensive income or loss, dividends, share repurchases, subsidiary stock sales, and other items; accompanying notes are referenced.

nodes.title: Consolidated Statements of Cash Flows
nodes.summary: Consolidated statements of cash flows for fiscal years ended January 31, 2022, 2021, and 2020, with amounts in millions. The statements detail operating cash flows, including net income, reconciliation adjustments, and changes in assets and liabilities; investing activities, including capital expenditures, asset disposals, acquisitions, and other items; financing activities, including borrowings, debt issuance and repayment, dividends, stock purchases, and other items; exchange-rate effects; changes in cash and restricted cash, reclassifications, and beginning and ending balances. Supplemental disclosures report income taxes and interest paid; accompanying notes are referenced.

Defines internal control over financial reporting, its reasonable-assurance objectives and limitations, and notes that effectiveness may weaken as conditions or compliance change; includes Ernst & Young LLP’s signed statement dated March 18, 2022. Presents Walmart’s consolidated financial statements for fiscal years 2020–2022: income, comprehensive income, balance sheets, shareholders’ equity, and cash flows, covering revenues, expenses, earnings, assets, liabilities, equity changes, operating, investing and financing cash flows, and supplemental disclosures, with references to accompanying notes.

summary: Ernst & Young’s independent report gives unqualified opinions on Walmart’s 2022 and 2021 consolidated financial statements and on the effectiveness of internal control over financial reporting as of January 31, 2022, under U.S. GAAP and COSO criteria. It describes management’s and the auditor’s responsibilities, PCAOB-compliant risk-based audit procedures, and internal-control objectives and limitations. Legal contingencies are identified as a critical audit matter, with procedures and judgments explained. The section also presents Walmart’s 2020–2022 consolidated financial statements and related notes and disclosures.

title: Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements

nodes.title: Note 1. Summary of Significant Accounting Policies
Walmart Accounting Policies and Cash
nodes.summary: Walmart describes its retail and eCommerce business and three reportable segments. Its consolidated statements cover fiscal 2020–2022, eliminate intercompany transactions, apply consolidation, variable-interest-entity and equity-method rules, and use differing reporting calendars for U.S./Canadian and other operations. U.S. GAAP estimates affect reported balances and results, which may differ from actual outcomes. Cash equivalents include investments with maturities of three months or less and card or electronic transactions settling within seven days; the text reports related balances, global cash holdings, and transfer restrictions. Receivables, net of doubtful-account reserves, arise from customers, suppliers, governments and real estate; customer receivables are reported for 2022 and 2021.

nodes.title: Receivables
nodes.summary: Walmart describes its customer-focused omnichannel business and three segments: U.S., International, and Sam’s Club. Its statements consolidate subsidiaries, eliminate intercompany items, account for certain entities using consolidation or the equity method, and use differing fiscal-year conventions; estimates follow U.S. GAAP. Policies cover cash equivalents, international cash and transfer restrictions; receivables and doubtful-account reserves; inventory valuation methods (LIFO, FIFO, and weighted average); held-for-sale presentation and prior-year U.K. and Japan disposals; property capitalization, depreciation, useful lives, balances, and expense; and lease identification, measurement, terms, short-term exemptions, and combined lease/non-lease components.

nodes.title: Inventory, Held-for-Sale Assets, Property, and Leases
nodes.summary: The page describes inventory valuation methods by business segment, including LIFO, FIFO, and weighted-average cost, and notes that LIFO values approximated FIFO in 2021 and 2022. Held-for-sale assets and liabilities are measured at the lower of carrying cost or fair value less selling costs and reviewed each period; 2022 balances were immaterial, while 2021 included U.K. and Japan operations sold in 2022. Property and equipment accounting, useful lives, balances, depreciation, and leasehold improvement amortization are outlined. Lease policies cover identifying leases, measuring right-of-use assets and obligations, determining terms and discount rates, short-term lease exemptions, and combining lease and non-lease components.

nodes.title: Asset Impairment, Goodwill, and Fair Value
key_items: Goodwill and Other Acquired Intangible Assets
nodes.summary: The page explains impairment reviews for long-lived assets and the accounting, allocation, and impairment testing of goodwill and acquired intangible assets. It reports goodwill balances and activity by segment, indefinite-lived intangible asset balances, and impairment charges. It defines fair value for assets and liabilities and describes accounting for equity and debt investments, including recurring fair-value changes and the cost approach for equity investments without readily determinable fair values.

nodes.title: Investments
nodes.summary: The text outlines accounting policies for long-lived asset impairment, goodwill and acquired intangibles, fair value, investments, indemnifications, self-insurance reserves, and derivatives. It describes impairment testing methods and reporting units; goodwill balances and activity by segment, including held-for-sale reclassifications, and intangible-asset balances and impairment history. It also explains investment measurement and income recognition, indemnity liabilities and maximum exposure, actuarial claims estimates and insurance protection, derivative credit-risk controls and accounting, and the treatment and maturities of fair-value and cash-flow hedges.

nodes.title: Indemnification Liabilities and Self-Insurance Reserves
nodes.summary: Trading debt securities are carried at fair value, with interest recorded as income; the company held $1.0 billion as of January 31, 2022. Divestiture-related legal and tax indemnification liabilities were $0.7 billion in 2022 and $0.6 billion in 2021, with maximum potential payments of $3.5 billion. The company self-insures several liability and employee healthcare risks, estimates claim and administrative costs using actuarial analysis, regularly reviews reserves, and limits exposure through insurance, including stop-loss coverage.

nodes.title: Derivatives
key_items: Fair Value Hedges; Cash Flow Hedges
nodes.summary: The text explains derivative use and risks, counterparty credit controls, collateral and netting, hedge-accounting criteria and balance-sheet presentation. It describes fair value swaps hedging fixed-rate debt, cash flow swaps hedging foreign-currency debt payments, and net investment hedges related to divested U.K. and Japan operations, including release of accumulated losses and prior debt balances. It outlines income-tax accounting, deferred-tax valuation, tax provisions, and uncertain tax benefits. Revenue policies cover merchandise and eCommerce sales and returns, membership fees and deferrals, gift-card redemption and breakage, and financial and other services.

nodes.title: Net Investment Hedges, Taxes, and Revenue Recognition
key_items: Net Sales; Membership Fee Revenue; Gift Cards; Financial and Other Services
nodes.summary: Describes former cross-currency swaps and foreign-currency debt hedging U.K. and Japan net investments, including release of accumulated losses after divestiture and $3.3 billion of designated debt at January 31, 2021. Explains income tax accounting, deferred taxes and valuation allowances, tax provisions, and uncertain tax benefits. Covers sales recognition, membership fees and deferrals, gift card redemption and estimated breakage, and recognition and classification of service revenue.

nodes.title: Expense Recognition and Currency Translation
key_items: Operating, Selling, General and Administrative Expenses
nodes.summary: Cost of sales covers product, transportation and specified warehousing costs, reduced by supplier payments that do not reimburse qualifying costs. Supplier consideration, including incentives and program reimbursements, generally reduces cost of sales and is recognized when related inventory is sold, except for reimbursements of specific, incremental, identifiable costs. Other operating costs are SG&A; distribution-cost classification differs by segment and can limit gross-profit comparisons. Advertising is expensed as incurred in SG&A and totaled $3.9 billion, $3.2 billion and $3.7 billion in fiscal 2022, 2021 and 2020. International assets and liabilities use period-end exchange rates, with adjustments in accumulated other comprehensive loss; income statements use average rates.

Walmart’s policies cover its business segments, consolidation, fiscal calendars, U.S. GAAP estimates, cash and receivables; inventory valuation, held-for-sale assets, property, depreciation and leases; impairment testing, goodwill, intangibles, fair value and investments; indemnifications and self-insurance; derivatives, hedge accounting, taxes and revenue recognition; cost of sales, supplier consideration, operating and advertising expenses; and foreign-currency translation. The section also reports related balances, charges, exposures, maturities and other financial details for fiscal 2020–2022.

nodes.title: Note 2. Net Income Per Common Share
nodes.summary: The note explains that basic Walmart earnings per share use weighted-average common shares, while diluted earnings per share also reflect dilutive share-based awards; no significant antidilutive awards were excluded in fiscal 2020–2022. A reconciliation presents consolidated net income, noncontrolling interests, net income attributable to Walmart, basic and diluted weighted-average shares, award dilution, and basic and diluted earnings per share for those fiscal years.

nodes.title: Note 3. Shareholders' Equity
nodes.summary: The note details Walmart’s common shares authorized and outstanding, $3.2 billion raised through Flipkart equity funding and the resulting ownership reduction, and share-based compensation expense and tax benefits for fiscal 2020–2022. It describes the 2015 Stock Incentive Plan, award types, vesting, valuation and expense recognition, Flipkart plans, award activity, vested fair values, unrecognized costs and remaining expense periods. It also explains the $20 billion repurchase program, decision factors, and shares, average prices and cash paid for repurchases across the three years.

nodes.title: Note 4. Accumulated Other Comprehensive Loss
nodes.summary: The note presents fiscal 2020–2022 changes in accumulated other comprehensive loss, by currency translation and other, net investment hedges, cash flow hedges, and minimum pension liability, including opening and closing balances, income or loss before reclassification, and amounts reclassified to income or related to business dispositions. Explanatory notes cover Asda pension remeasurement, the $0.8 billion untaxed currency-translation loss on the sale of most of Walmart Argentina, and releases upon U.K. and Japan business sales. Derivative reclassifications are recorded in interest, net; pension and business-disposition translation amounts are recorded in other gains and losses.

nodes.title: Note 5. Accrued Liabilities
nodes.summary: The note reports accrued liabilities of $26.060 billion at January 31, 2022, versus $37.966 billion in 2021. Categories include wages and benefits, self-insurance, non-income taxes, deferred gift-card revenue, liabilities held for sale, and other accrued liabilities. Wages and benefits cover pay, vacation, bonuses, and incentives; self-insurance includes workers’ compensation, liability, and certain healthcare costs; taxes include payroll, property, VAT, sales, and other taxes. 2021 held-for-sale liabilities relate to Japan and U.K. operations. Other items include deferred membership revenue, interest, advertising, maintenance and utilities, and supply chain.

nodes.title: Note 6. Short-term Borrowings and Long-term Debt
nodes.summary: Note 6 details short-term borrowings, committed credit facilities, letters of credit, long-term debt balances and rates for 2022 and 2021, debt maturities, and related covenants and fees. It summarizes fiscal 2022 debt issuances, including a green bond, and fiscal 2022 and 2021 matured and extinguished debt repayments. The company recorded a $2.4 billion fiscal 2022 extinguishment loss, including $2.3 billion in early repayment premiums.

nodes.title: Note 7. Leases
nodes.summary: Note 7 describes the Company’s leases of retail, distribution, warehouse, office, land, and equipment assets in the U.S. and internationally. It presents 2020–2022 operating, finance, and variable lease costs; lease-related cash payments and assets obtained; remaining lease terms and discount rates as of January 31, 2021 and 2022; and operating and finance lease obligations by fiscal year through 2027 and thereafter, including total undiscounted obligations, imputed interest, and net obligations.

nodes.title: Note 8. Fair Value Measurements
nodes.summary: The note explains the fair value hierarchy (Levels 1–3) and reports recurring fair values for equity investments, plus Level 2 derivative valuations based on interest-rate and foreign-currency curves, with notional amounts, fair values, and balance-sheet classifications. Nonrecurring measurements cover impairment charges: $0.4 billion on Asda and Seiyu sales in fiscal 2022; fiscal 2021 disposal-group impairments for Argentina, Japan, and the U.K. within an $8.3 billion divestiture loss (including a $2.3 billion Asda pension charge); and fiscal 2020 write-downs of eCommerce assets and Jabong.com. Other impairments were immaterial. Short-term instruments are carried at cost, approximating fair value; long-term debt is carried at cost, with Level 2 fair value estimates and 2022/2021 carrying and fair values disclosed.

nodes.title: Note 9. Taxes
Note 9. Taxes (intro)
nodes.summary: Note 9 presents income before taxes by U.S. and non-U.S. sources for fiscal 2020–2022, and the income tax provision by current and deferred U.S. federal, state and local, and international components. It reconciles the U.S. statutory rate to effective tax rates, identifying state taxes, foreign income, business wind-downs, valuation allowances, repatriated earnings, tax credits, tax-law changes, tax contingency reserves, and other items. Subsequent disclosures on deferred taxes, unremitted earnings, loss and credit carryforwards, valuation allowances, and uncertain tax positions exclude held-for-sale operations.

nodes.title: Deferred Taxes
nodes.summary: The text reports the Company’s deferred tax balances in millions for January 31, 2022 and 2021. It lists deferred tax assets by category, valuation allowances, net deferred tax assets, deferred tax liabilities by category, and net deferred tax liabilities. It also shows balance-sheet classification: deferred tax assets within other long-term assets and deferred tax liabilities within deferred income taxes and other, with the resulting net liabilities for each year.

nodes.title: Foreign Earnings and Income Tax Matters
key_items: Net Operating Losses, Tax Credit Carryforwards and Valuation Allowances
nodes.summary: The page covers foreign earnings, tax carryforwards, valuation allowances, and uncertain tax positions. Most previously unremitted foreign earnings were taxed under the 2017 Tax Act; remaining indefinitely reinvested earnings carry about $3 billion in unrecorded deferred tax liabilities. Loss and capital-loss carryforwards total $39.3 billion, with $26.6 billion expiring by 2042; valuation allowances were $9.5 billion in 2022 versus $8.8 billion in 2021. It describes allowance assessment, unrecognized tax benefits and their reconciliation, related interest and penalties, possible audit-resolution effects, and tax examination periods.

nodes.title: Other Taxes
nodes.summary: The Company faces examinations of value-added, sales-based, payroll, and other non-income taxes in various jurisdictions; some have resulted in assessments or judgments. Individual potential losses are generally immaterial, but adverse outcomes across related matters could create a liability material to the consolidated financial statements.

Note 9 details fiscal 2020–2022 income before taxes by U.S. and foreign sources, tax provisions and statutory-to-effective-rate reconciliations. It presents deferred tax assets and liabilities and their balance-sheet classifications; discusses foreign earnings and unrecorded deferred taxes, loss and credit carryforwards, valuation allowances, unrecognized tax benefits, related interest and penalties, audits, and examination periods; and describes non-income-tax examinations and assessments, which are generally individually immaterial but could collectively result in a material liability.

nodes.title: Note 10. Contingencies
nodes.summary: The Company describes legal proceedings and regulatory matters, recording accruals when appropriate and disclosing reasonably possible material liabilities; adverse outcomes or settlements could materially affect its finances. Opioid matters include multidistrict and state litigation, a 2021 adverse jury liability verdict with damages proceedings and an intended appeal, government investigations, a dismissed-and-affirmed declaratory action, a stayed DOJ enforcement case, consolidated securities class actions, and shareholder derivative suits. Losses cannot be estimated, and the Company intends to defend vigorously. Asda faces UK employee equal-value claims; after its 2021 divestiture, the Company oversees the defense and provides capped contractual indemnification, but losses and outcomes cannot be estimated.

nodes.title: Note 11. Retirement-Related Benefits
nodes.summary: The Company provides U.S. and Puerto Rico 401(k) plans, with different eligibility start dates; after one year, it matches 100% of contributions up to 6% of eligible earnings, immediately vested, while participant contributions are capped at 50% of pretax earnings and statutory limits. Non-U.S. international associates participate in locally administered defined-contribution plans. The text reports contribution expenses for fiscal 2020–2022. It also describes Asda’s former U.K. defined-benefit plan: a $1.0 billion 2020 contribution funded bulk annuity insurance and ended future obligations; $2.3 billion of accumulated pension components entered the sale disposal group, with a pre-tax loss recognized in fiscal 2021.

nodes.title: Note 12. Disposals, Acquisitions and Related Items
nodes.summary: The note details Walmart International disposals. Asda was sold in February 2021 for $9.6 billion, with a $0.2 billion closing loss after a $5.5 billion estimated loss in fiscal 2021; Walmart deconsolidated it, retained a debt security, and recorded indemnity liabilities. Seiyu was sold in March 2021 for $1.2 billion, with a $0.2 billion closing loss after a $1.9 billion estimated loss; Walmart retained a 15% equity interest. The note lists January 2021 assets and liabilities held for sale for both groups and explains valuation adjustments, pension derecognition, currency impacts, and included balance-sheet items. Walmart Argentina’s November 2020 sale generated a $1.0 billion loss, mainly from cumulative currency translation losses. Other immaterial transactions occurred or were announced.

nodes.title: Note 13. Segments and Disaggregated Revenue
nodes.summary: The note describes Walmart’s three reportable segments—U.S., International and Sam’s Club—their operations, CODM-based performance measures, and Corporate and support. It presents segment financial results and consolidated reconciliations for fiscal 2020–2022, plus U.S./non-U.S. revenue and long-lived assets, noting no material single-country or customer concentration and excluding held-for-sale assets. It also disaggregates segment net sales by merchandise category or market and reports eCommerce sales for each segment across the three years.

nodes.title: Note 14. Subsequent Event
nodes.summary: The Board approved a fiscal 2023 annual dividend of $2.24 per share, up from $2.20 in fiscal 2022, payable in four $0.56 quarterly installments. Record/payable dates are March 18/April 4, 2022; May 6/May 31, 2022; August 12/September 6, 2022; and December 9, 2022/January 3, 2023.

summary: The notes explain Walmart’s significant accounting policies and provide fiscal 2020–2022 financial disclosures on earnings per share; shareholders’ equity, share-based compensation and repurchases; comprehensive loss; accrued liabilities; borrowings, debt and leases; fair-value measurements and impairments; income and other taxes; legal and regulatory contingencies; retirement benefits; and disposals, acquisitions and related items. They also describe reportable segments, revenue and geographic information, and the subsequent approval and payment schedule of the fiscal 2023 dividend.

title: Accountants, Controls, and Other Disclosures
key_items: ITEM 9. CHANGES IN AND DISAGREEMENTS WITH ACCOUNTANTS ON ACCOUNTING AND FINANCIAL DISCLOSURE

summary: Reports no disagreements with accountants. Management evaluates disclosure controls as effective, while noting reasonable-assurance limits and reduced control over unconsolidated entities. Internal control over financial reporting was assessed as effective under the COSO 2013 framework as of January 31, 2022, and audited by Ernst & Young. Routine control improvements had no material effect, and no material changes occurred. Other information is none; foreign-jurisdiction inspection disclosure is not applicable.

ITEM 12. SECURITY OWNERSHIP OF CERTAIN BENEFICIAL OWNERS AND MANAGEMENT AND RELATED STOCKHOLDER MATTERS
ITEM 13. CERTAIN RELATIONSHIPS AND RELATED TRANSACTIONS, AND DIRECTOR INDEPENDENCE
summary: Part III identifies where the filing or 2022 proxy statement provides information on executive officers, directors and family relationships, audit committee and financial experts, senior financial officer reporting protocols, code of conduct, executive and director compensation, stock ownership, related transactions, and director independence. It notes that shareholder director-nomination procedures have not materially changed since the 2021 proxy statement, and describes website availability of conduct and reporting protocols and related amendments or waivers.

title: ITEM 14. PRINCIPAL ACCOUNTING FEES AND SERVICES
summary: Item 14 incorporates the proxy statement’s discussion of independent-accountant ratification and fees. Item 15 identifies the financial statements in Item 8, explains that no financial statement schedules are included because they are unnecessary or their information appears elsewhere, and lists exhibits filed or incorporated by reference. These include corporate charter and bylaws, debt indentures and securities descriptions, compensation and benefit plans, executive agreements, Flipkart transaction agreements, subsidiaries, auditor consent, officer certifications, opioid-litigation information, Inline XBRL files, and the cover-page data file. Notes identify newly filed or furnished exhibits, compensatory plans, paper-filed exhibits, and omitted debt instruments available to the SEC on request. No financial statement schedules are listed.
