summary: Item 16 states that Walmart has no Form 10-K summary. The signatures section records Walmart Inc.’s Form 10-K, signed March 18, 2022, by CEO C. Douglas McMillon and, in their stated capacities, chairman Gregory B. Penner, CFO M. Brett Biggs, controller David M. Chojnowski, and directors Cesar Conde, Timothy P. Flynn, Sarah Friar, Carla A. Harris, Thomas W. Horton, Marissa A. Mayer, Steven S. Reinemund, Randall L. Stephenson, S. Robson Walton, and Steuart L. Walton. The report covers the fiscal year ended January 31, 2022; Exhibit 10.1 follows.

title: WALMART DEFERRED COMPENSATION MATCHING PLAN
summary: Table of contents for Walmart’s Deferred Compensation Matching Plan, amended and restated effective November 11, 2021. It covers general provisions and definitions; deferred compensation and bonus credits, employer matching credits, allocation elections and suspensions; account credits, valuation and earnings; benefit payments for scheduled in-service events, separation, death, emergencies and taxes, including distribution forms and misconduct reductions; administration and delegation; claims and appeals, including disability claims; and miscellaneous rules on amendment or termination, non-alienation, overpayments, employment and bonus rights, taxes, successors, and governing law.

title: WALMART DEFERRED COMPENSATION
key_items: 1.1 Purpose.; 1.2 Effective Date.; 1.3 Nature of Plan.
summary: The Walmart Deferred Compensation Matching Plan lets certain individuals defer compensation and receive matching allocations and earnings, rewarding contributions and supporting retirement savings beyond 401(k) limits. Its amended and restated effective date is November 11, 2021. It is an unfunded ERISA plan for select management or highly compensated employees, paid solely from Walmart’s general assets; participants have only unsecured-creditor rights, with no claim to specific assets, trust, or fiduciary relationship created. The Plan must comply with and be administered under Code Section 409A.

title: ARTICLE II. DEFINITIONS
summary: Defines the Plan’s key terms, including participant accounts and their pre-2021/post-2020 class, deferral, matching, retirement, and in-service subaccounts; compensation, deferrals, credits, bonuses, and employer matches; eligibility rules for officers and participants; employers, related affiliates, and governing tax and benefits laws; excess compensation and gross misconduct; plan administration and year; scheduled payment dates, separation from service and payment dates, disability, emergencies, and special bonuses; valuation dates, Walmart, and years of participation.

title: ARTICLE III. DEFERRAL CREDITS AND MATCHING CONTRIBUTION CREDITS AND ACCOUNT ALLOCATIONS

nodes.title: 3.1 Deferred Compensation.
nodes.summary: Eligible Officers may defer some or all compensation, capped at 80% for Plan Years beginning February 1, 2022, while retaining enough for required taxes, premiums, and permitted withholdings. Deferrals are prorated by payroll period; periods spanning Plan Years follow the election for the year in which they end. Elections must use Administrator-approved forms and be filed by December 31 for existing participants, or within 30 days of becoming eligible if specified 409A aggregation and prior-participation conditions are met. New-eligibility elections apply only to later payroll periods and must satisfy Section 409A. Deferred amounts are credited to the officer’s Deferral Account and allocated to a Retirement or Scheduled In-Service Account under Section 3.5.

nodes.title: 3.2 Deferred MIP Bonuses
nodes.summary: Eligible Participants may defer all or part of an MIP bonus for a performance period coinciding with or ending in a Plan Year; non-officers may defer at most 80%. Deferrals cannot reduce pay below required tax, insurance, or other permitted withholdings, and must use Plan Administrator-approved forms. Elections are generally due by the preceding December 31, with alternatives for qualifying performance-based bonuses and newly eligible officers subject to 409A conditions. A new officer’s election applies only to post-election services, prorated by remaining performance-period days. Deferred bonuses are credited to the participant’s Plan Year Deferral Account and allocated to a Retirement or Scheduled In-Service Account under Section 3.5.

nodes.title: 3.3 Deferred Special Bonuses.
nodes.summary: Eligible Officers may defer all or part of a Special Bonus using an Administrator-approved (including electronic) form. Elections cannot reduce pay below required taxes, insurance premiums, or other permitted withholdings; the election date is when the Administrator receives the executed form. Deferral is allowed only for qualifying bonuses: (1) service-conditioned bonuses requiring at least 13 months’ continued service, with no earlier vesting for good-reason termination or retirement and meeting Code Section 409A requirements, elected within 30 days of obtaining a binding right; or (2) bonuses under a pre-employment, written-accepted offer letter explicitly referencing Plan deferral, elected before any services begin. Deferred amounts are credited to the officer’s Deferral Account and allocated to a Retirement or Scheduled In-Service Account under Section 3.5.

nodes.title: 3.4 Employer Matching Contribution Credits
nodes.summary: Eligible participants employed by the Employer or a Related Affiliate on the Plan Year’s last day, with no separation during that year and qualifying deferrals, receive a matching credit equal to deferred compensation and MIP bonus deferrals, capped at 6% of Excess Compensation. No match applies to deferrals withdrawn under Section 5.5; credits are allocated under Section 3.5. Matching accounts and earnings vest after three Years of Participation, or earlier upon death before separation or disability. Distribution under Article V requires vesting as of separation.

nodes.title: 3.5 Account Allocation Elections
nodes.summary: Participants must allocate each deferral to a Retirement or Scheduled In-Service Account and allocate related employer matching credits to a Retirement Account. Their first Retirement Account allocation requires choosing a permitted distribution form; their first Scheduled In-Service allocation requires choosing a Scheduled Pay Date. If no allocation is elected, the prior Plan Year’s allocation for the same category applies. If none exists, pre-February 1, 2021 amounts go to the applicable Pre-2021 Retirement Account(s), equally if multiple, or to a deemed permitted Retirement Account with lump-sum payment; amounts for later Plan Years go to a deemed Retirement Account under the applicable Class Account with lump-sum payment.

nodes.title: 3.6 Irrevocability of Deferral Elections and Account Allocation Elections
nodes.summary: Deferral and related account-allocation elections generally become irrevocable after their specified filing deadline or election date, do not carry over to later Plan Years, and require a new election. Section 3.1 elections end at separation (covering the last regular paycheck) but resume if rehired in the same year; Sections 3.2–3.3 bonus elections remain applicable to the covered bonus, including after qualifying rehire. Loss of officer status ends Section 3.1 elections the following January 31, with reduced compensation prorated; short-term disability-related reductions are also prorated. Loss of participant status ends Section 3.2 elections for performance periods starting the next calendar year, while Section 3.3 elections continue after loss of officer status. Unpaid leave suspends Section 3.1 elections, which resume upon same-year return; they still apply to covered compensation paid during leave, and leave does not affect Sections 3.2–3.3 elections.

nodes.title: 3.7 Automatic Suspension of Deferral Elections
nodes.summary: If a participant seeks a distribution or deferral cancellation due to an Unforeseeable Emergency, and the Plan Administrator or delegate determines stopping deferrals may relieve it, some or all deferral elections under Sections 3.1–3.3 for that Plan Year are cancelled as soon as administratively practicable.

summary: The Article governs compensation, MIP bonus, and qualifying Special Bonus deferrals, including eligibility, limits, withholding protections, election forms and deadlines, prorating, Section 409A conditions, and account credits. It sets employer matching-credit eligibility, limits, allocation, and vesting; requires allocation to Retirement or Scheduled In-Service Accounts and provides defaults for missing elections. It also addresses election irrevocability, effects of separation, rehire, status changes, disability, and unpaid leave, and automatic suspension of deferrals when needed to address an Unforeseeable Emergency.

title: ARTICLE IV. ACCOUNTS AND TIMING OF CREDITS TO ACCOUNTS
key_items: 4.1 Nature of Accounts.; 4.2 Deferral Credits and Employer Matching Contribution Credits.; 4.3 Valuation of Accounts.
4.2 Deferral Credits and Employer Matching Contribution Credits.
summary: Participant accounts are bookkeeping measures only, not participant property or trusts; all credited amounts remain Walmart’s property, and benefits are an unsecured promise payable under the Plan. Deferral and bonus credits enter the applicable Deferral Account after they otherwise would have been paid, while matching credits enter the Matching Account at the Plan Year’s end. The administrator maintains accounts, including earnings, until benefits are fully paid. Accounts are valued monthly and credited monthly with interest based on the 10-year Treasury yield set on the first January business day plus 270 basis points, using Federal Reserve H-15 or another Committee-selected source; interest is simple for each month, calculated on the prior valuation balance, and thus compounds monthly.

title: ARTICLE V. PAYMENT OF PLAN BENEFITS

nodes.title: 5.1 Scheduled In-Service Benefits.
nodes.summary: Scheduled in-service accounts are paid as a lump sum within 90 days after the applicable Scheduled Pay Date, based on their value on that date. If a separation or death triggers an earlier distribution under Section 5.2 or 5.3, the account is distributed under that section instead.

nodes.title: 5.2 Separation Benefits.
nodes.summary: Upon separation from service, Scheduled In-Service Accounts are paid in a lump sum, while Retirement Accounts follow the participant’s effective distribution election: lump sum or annual installments. Lump sums are paid within 90 days after the Separation Pay Date and valued as of the prior month-end. Installments begin within 90 days after the applicable January 31, or after the Separation Pay Date if that date comes first; later installments follow each successive January 31. Equal annual payments are calculated to amortize the account’s lump-sum value over the installment period, with interest at the Plan Year rate for the year of separation.

nodes.title: 5.3 Death Benefits.
nodes.summary: If a participant dies before separation or benefit commencement, the account is paid under the effective election: one form must apply to all beneficiary levels, and no effective election defaults to a lump sum. Lump sums are paid within 90 days after the month of death, based on the account value at the prior month-end. Annual installments begin within 90 days of the first January 31 on or after death, then recur annually; equal payments amortize the account value over the elected period at the Plan Year death-year interest rate. After installments begin, payments continue to the beneficiary in the same form, unless the election is lump sum, in which case the remainder is paid within 90 days after the death month. Participants may file and change written or electronic primary and contingent beneficiary designations, including trusts, and specify shares. Without eligible designations, payment follows the stated priority: surviving spouse, children, parents, siblings, then estate. If a beneficiary dies before full payment, benefits pass equally to remaining beneficiaries at that level, then to the next level; if none remain, the deceased beneficiary’s spouse, children, parents, siblings, or estate receive them in that order.

nodes.title: 5.4 Forms of Distribution.
nodes.summary: Upon separation from service, or death before separation, participants may elect a lump sum, up to 15 years of substantially equal annual installments, or—only for death distributions—a combination, subject to a $50,000 minimum. The threshold applies to the relevant Pre-2021 account or combined Post-2020 installment accounts; below it, payment defaults to a lump sum when the first installment would otherwise be due. Elections may be changed under rules requiring a 12-month wait, generally a five-year payment delay, 12 months’ advance notice, and completion by the end of the Plan Year containing the 20th anniversary of separation or death; death is exempt from the delay. Installments count as one payment for these rules. Invalid elections are disregarded in favor of the most recent valid election. Elections and scheduled in-service pay dates must be filed on administrator-prescribed forms.

nodes.title: 5.5 Distributions for Unforeseeable Emergencies.
nodes.summary: Upon written application, the Plan Administrator may, in its sole discretion, approve an emergency distribution to a participant or eligible beneficiary, excluding unvested matching-account amounts. Payments are limited to the amount needed for the emergency and anticipated taxes and penalties, after considering insurance, asset liquidation, and stopping deferrals. Funds are drawn first from current-year scheduled in-service accounts, then current-year retirement accounts, then proportionally from remaining balances in those account types. For distributions before January 1, 2021, payment must be suspended to the extent a Code Section 162(m) deduction is expected to be barred, until deduction is expected to be permitted and emergency conditions still apply.

nodes.title: Tax Distributions and Gross Misconduct Reductions
key_items: 5.7 Reductions Arising from a Participant’s Gross Misconduct.
nodes.summary: The Plan Administrator may pay a lump sum from benefits to cover applicable FICA, withholding, and state, local, or foreign taxes arising from Plan participation. Benefits are contingent on avoiding Gross Misconduct during employment or any additional period under Walmart’s Statement of Ethics. If misconduct is determined, matching credits and their earnings are forfeited, and deferral-account earnings and remaining installments are recalculated at half the applicable annual rate; deferred compensation and specified deferred bonuses cannot be forfeited. If misconduct is found after payment, the participant or beneficiary must repay amounts exceeding entitlement.

summary: The article governs payment of plan benefits: scheduled in-service distributions; separation and death benefits, including lump sums, installments, timing, valuation, interest, elections, and beneficiary designations and succession; permitted distribution forms, minimums, election changes, and filing rules; discretionary emergency distributions and payment priorities, including a historical tax-deduction restriction; tax-withholding distributions; and forfeitures, reductions, and repayment obligations tied to Gross Misconduct, with specified protections for deferred compensation and bonuses.

title: ARTICLE VI. ADMINISTRATION
key_items: 6.1 General.; 6.2 Allocation and Delegation of Duties.
summary: The Plan Administrator administers the Plan, with exclusive authority to interpret its terms, decide benefit eligibility and amounts, resolve participant disputes, and adopt or change operating rules. It may appoint assistants and establish forms. Its decisions bind affected parties, subject to Article VII’s claims procedure. When its own Plan rights or benefits are at issue, the Committee performs these duties and the Administrator cannot participate or vote. The Administrator may delegate and revoke responsibilities in writing; delegates’ actions have equivalent effect, delegates must report periodically, and the Administrator is not liable for their acts or omissions.

title: ARTICLE VII. CLAIMS PROCEDURE
summary: Benefit claims must be filed in writing within one year after separation from service; late claims forfeit all rights. Initial denials must be issued within 60 days, or up to 120 days when special circumstances apply, and explain the reasons, relevant Plan provisions, needed information, review process, and ERISA suit rights. Claimants may appeal in writing within 60 days, review relevant documents, and submit comments. Appeal decisions are due within 60 days, or up to 120 days for special circumstances, and must explain the determination, cite Plan provisions, describe access to relevant records and any voluntary appeals, and state ERISA suit rights. Disability claims follow the cited DOL regulation.

title: ARTICLE VIII. MISCELLANEOUS PROVISIONS

nodes.title: 8.1 Amendment, Suspension or Termination of Plan.
nodes.summary: Walmart, through the Committee, may amend, suspend, or terminate the Plan, but cannot do so to forfeit participants’ existing Accounts. Around a Code Section 409A change in control of a relevant affiliate, it may partially terminate the Plan and distribute benefits to affected participants within 12 months, provided all required aggregated plans are also terminated and liquidated for those participants. All actions must comply with Section 409A.

nodes.title: Plan Rights, Payments, and Taxes
nodes.summary: Plan benefits generally cannot be transferred or seized, except for a single lump-sum distribution under a qualifying domestic relations order. Recipients must repay mistaken overpayments when Walmart requests. The Plan grants no employment rights or entitlement to bonuses, which are governed by applicable bonus arrangements. Employers withhold legally required employment and income taxes; participants or beneficiaries are responsible for all resulting income and excise taxes.

title: COUNTRY-SPECIFIC APPENDIX

nodes.title: COUNTRY-SPECIFIC APPENDIX (intro)
nodes.summary: The appendix explains that undefined capitalized terms follow the Plan or PRSU terms, and adds country-specific conditions for participants based on their work or residence; Walmart determines applicability in cross-border or changed-status situations. Its legal and exchange-control notices reflect laws as of December 2021, may become outdated or not fit individual circumstances, and warrant professional advice. In Argentina, PRSUs and shares are not publicly offered or exchange-listed or registered, and participation is through a private offering outside Argentina. Participants must comply with currency restrictions, approvals, and reporting rules; Argentine tax residents must report plan shares held in foreign bank accounts on December 31 in their annual tax return.

nodes.title: BRAZIL
nodes.summary: Brazilian PRSU terms require compliance with applicable law and payment of related taxes on awards, share sales, and dividends. Acceptance confirms an investment decision; shares issue only upon vesting, and their value may rise or fall without compensation. Foreign assets exceeding reporting thresholds require annual Central Bank declarations, with quarterly reporting above US$100 million; Brazilian visa holders are treated as residents, and thresholds may change. PRSU income must be reported on the DIRPF. Repatriated funds and currency conversions may incur IOF, which participants must pay.

nodes.summary: Canadian PRSU terms address suspension and resumption or forfeiture of vesting during administrative suspension; exclusion of awards from regular compensation; limits on claims for forfeiture; termination-date rules, statutory notice exceptions, and no prorated vesting or lost-vesting compensation; and discretionary cash, share, or mixed settlement, including open-market purchases through a broker. Quebec residents acknowledge English-language documents. Data privacy consent permits information sharing and employee-file retention. Notices cover permitted share resales outside Canada through a listed exchange and annual T1135 reporting thresholds and share cost-base rules.

nodes.title: CHILE
nodes.summary: For Chile, PRSUs, underlying shares, and related income or value are excluded from the remuneration base for statutory or contractual severance and pay in lieu of notice. The grant is a private securities offering under CMF General Ruling 336; the securities are unregistered, not CMF-supervised, require no public disclosure, and cannot be publicly offered until registered (explained in English and Spanish). Repatriation is optional, but amounts exceeding US$10,000 must use the Formal Exchange Market. Foreign investments exceeding US$5 million in a calendar year must be reported to the Central Bank. CIRS electronic sworn statements on foreign investment results and taxes paid are due before July 1; failure may affect foreign tax credits. Requirements may change; consult legal and tax advisers.

nodes.title: HONG KONG
nodes.summary: Hong Kong terms specify that PRSU shares are personal investments and, if delivered within six months of the grant date, cannot be publicly offered or disposed of before that anniversary. PRSUs settle only in shares, not cash. They are not a public securities offering, are available only to eligible Walmart or affiliate employees, and related documents are not prospectuses, have not been regulator-reviewed, and are for recipients’ personal use only; recipients uncertain about their contents should seek independent advice. Walmart intends the Plan not to qualify as an occupational retirement scheme under Hong Kong law.

nodes.title: INDIA
nodes.summary: India: PRSUs, underlying shares, and related income/value are extraordinary and excluded from annual gross salary. Indian exchange-control residents must repatriate sale proceeds within the legally prescribed period, obtain and retain an FIRC as evidence, and tax residents must report foreign bank accounts and financial assets in annual tax returns, consulting a tax adviser. Japan: tax residents must report foreign assets exceeding ¥50 million as of December 31 by March 15, and acquisitions of shares worth over ¥100 million in one transaction require a Securities Acquisition Report within 20 days; tax advice is recommended. Luxembourg has no country-specific provisions. Mexico: PRSU grants are discretionary; Plan or Agreement changes or termination do not impair Continuous Status, and Walmart may amend or discontinue awards without liability. Walmart is identified as Plan administrator, with its Bentonville address.

nodes.title: Country-Specific Financial Reporting Requirements
nodes.summary: The text advises Indian tax residents to retain a bank-issued FIRC as evidence of fund repatriation and to report foreign accounts and financial assets in annual tax returns. Japanese tax residents may need to report foreign assets exceeding ¥50 million as of December 31 by March 15, including relevant plan holdings; acquisitions of shares worth over ¥100 million in one transaction require a Securities Acquisition Report within 20 days. Luxembourg has no country-specific provisions.

nodes.title: MEXICO
nodes.summary: Mexico-specific PRSU terms supplement Paragraph 13: accepting PRSUs acknowledges that plan changes or termination do not affect employment status; awards are discretionary and may be changed or ended without liability; participation is commercial, not employment, and Walmart administers the Plan. Recipients confirm reviewing and accepting the documents, acknowledge participation is voluntary, creates no acquired right, and carries no responsibility for share-value decreases, and release Walmart and affiliates from related claims. A Spanish translation repeats these provisions. Securities notices state PRSUs and shares are unregistered and cannot be publicly offered or sold in Mexico; plan materials cannot be publicly distributed or copied. The offer is a private placement to current employees under Mexican law, and associated rights cannot be transferred.

nodes.title: PERU
nodes.summary: Peru: PRSUs are granted ex gratia as a reward; the offer is a private offering exempt from registration, with further details in Walmart’s plan and grant documents. South Africa: PRSUs and shares are not publicly offered or exchange-listed; the private offer is under Companies Act Section 96, requires acceptance or rejection within 60 days of the grant date, and is deemed accepted if not declined. Recipients must report vesting income to Walmart or their employer and may face recovery of employer penalties or interest, or a fine, for failure to report. Recipients are responsible for complying with changing exchange-control rules and should consult a personal adviser.

nodes.title: UNITED KINGDOM
nodes.summary: The UK terms supplement Paragraph 10 on taxes and withholding: the participant must pay all tax-related amounts when requested and indemnify Walmart and its affiliates for amounts they pay or withhold. Directors or executive officers may be unable to indemnify unpaid income tax if that would constitute a loan; the unpaid tax may then be a taxable benefit subject to income tax and employee National Insurance. The participant must report and pay the additional income tax to HMRC under self-assessment and reimburse Walmart or the employer for related National Insurance contributions, recoverable through Paragraph 10 methods.

nodes.title: UNITED STATES
nodes.summary: U.S. terms address military leave and data privacy. If an employee is on the same military leave on the grant and vesting dates, continuous status must be maintained for at least six months after returning before the award vests; the vesting date is deemed six months after return, and adjusted PRSU shares are delivered as soon as administratively feasible, no later than 74 days after vesting. The data privacy provision supplements Paragraph 15 and links to Walmart’s California Consumer Privacy Act policies. Employees with visual disabilities should contact HR for accommodations.

summary: The appendix applies Plan definitions and country-specific terms according to work or residence, with Walmart resolving cross-border or status questions; legal notices reflect December 2021 and advise professional counsel. It covers private-offering and securities restrictions, taxes and withholding, exchange controls, foreign-asset reporting, settlement and vesting, employment and severance treatment, data privacy, language consent, and participant acknowledgments or liabilities. Argentina, Brazil, Canada, Chile, Guatemala, Hong Kong, India, Japan, Mexico, Peru, South Africa, the UK, and the US have specific provisions; Costa Rica, Luxembourg, and Nigeria have none.

title: Significant Subsidiaries of Walmart Inc.
summary: The document lists Walmart Inc.’s significant subsidiaries, explaining that omitted subsidiaries are not significant in the aggregate under Regulation S-K Item 601(b)(21). It identifies each subsidiary’s legal name, jurisdiction of organization, business name (where different), and Walmart’s ownership percentage. Listed entities are organized in the United States, Mexico, Canada, Singapore, Chile, South Africa, and the Cayman Islands, with ownership ranging from 53% to 100%. A note states that Walmart owns substantially all of Walmart Chile.

title: Consent of Independent Registered Public Accounting Firm

nodes.title: Consent of Independent Registered Public Accounting Firm (intro)
nodes.summary: Ernst & Young LLP consents to incorporating its March 18, 2022 reports on Walmart Inc.’s consolidated financial statements and internal control over financial reporting into 18 listed registration statements (Forms S-3, S-3ASR, and S-8) covering company stock, debt securities, investment, compensation, incentive, associate stock purchase, retirement savings, profit-sharing, and deferred-compensation plans. The consent is signed in Rogers, Arkansas, on March 18, 2022.

nodes.title: Exhibit 31.1
nodes.summary: In Exhibit 31.1, Walmart CEO C. Douglas McMillon certifies that he reviewed the company’s Form 10-K; that, to his knowledge, it contains no materially misleading statements and fairly presents the company’s financial condition, results and cash flows; and that he and the other certifying officer oversee disclosure controls and financial reporting controls, including their design, evaluation and reporting of material changes. They also report significant control deficiencies or weaknesses and any fraud involving employees with key control roles to the auditors and Audit Committee. Signed March 18, 2022.

nodes.title: Exhibit 31.2
nodes.summary: Exhibit 31.2 is CFO M. Brett Biggs’s March 18, 2022 certification regarding Walmart’s Form 10-K. He confirms he reviewed the report, that it contains no materially misleading statements or omissions, and that its financial information fairly presents the company’s condition, results, and cash flows. He and the other certifying officer attest to responsibility for designing, evaluating, and reporting on disclosure controls and financial reporting controls, including material quarterly changes, and confirm they disclosed significant control deficiencies or weaknesses and relevant fraud to the auditors and Audit Committee.

title: CERTIFICATION PURSUANT TO 18 U.S.C. SECTION 1350 (AS ADOPTED PURSUANT TO SECTION 906 OF THE SARBANES-OXLEY ACT OF 2002)

nodes.title: CERTIFICATION PURSUANT TO 18 U.S.C. SECTION 1350 (AS ADOPTED PURSUANT TO SECTION 906 OF THE SARBANES-OXLEY ACT OF 2002) (intro)
nodes.summary: Walmart CEO C. Douglas McMillon and CFO M. Brett Biggs each certify under Sarbanes-Oxley Section 906 that the company’s Form 10-K for the year ended January 31, 2022 complies with applicable Securities Exchange Act reporting requirements and fairly presents Walmart’s financial condition and operating results. Both certificates are effective March 18, 2022. The text also identifies an exhibit listing state-court opioid litigation case citations and currently scheduled trial dates.

nodes.title: A. Case Citations For Pending State Court Cases as of March 4, 2022
nodes.summary: A chronological citation list, current as of March 4, 2022, of pending state-court opioid-related lawsuits filed from 2017–2022. Cases involve states, counties, cities, towns, hospitals, health organizations, and an individual minor suing pharmaceutical manufacturers, distributors, pharmacies, and Sackler-related parties. Citations identify plaintiffs, defendants, courts and jurisdictions, and filing dates across numerous states, especially West Virginia, New York, South Carolina, and Pennsylvania.

nodes.title: B. Currently Scheduled Trial Dates In Pending State Court Cases as of March 4, 2022
nodes.summary: Lists seven scheduled trial dates, as of March 4, 2022, in pending state court cases: New Mexico v. Purdue Pharma (Sept. 6, 2022); West Virginia v. Walmart (Sept. 12, 2022); Mobile County Board of Health v. Richard Sackler (Jan. 9, 2023); DCH Health Care Authority v. Purdue Pharma (Mar. 20, 2023; limited to public-nuisance liability); Jefferson County v. Williams (Apr. 4, 2023); Nevada v. McKesson (Apr. 17, 2023); and Lester E. Cox Medical Centers v. Amneal Pharmaceuticals (Oct. 14, 2024).
